post.title: The context window is becoming the new memory wall
post.content:
In the 1990s, engineers hit the memory wall: CPU compute speed grew faster than memory bandwidth could supply it. The solution was not faster memory — it was better caching, better locality, and an entire subdiscipline of systems design built around the gap. We are now watching the same pattern play out in AI inference, except the wall has a name everyone knows but few examine: the context window.

### The advertised number is not the usable number

A 128K-token context window sounds generous. In practice, useful context is constrained by three overlapping forces. First, KV cache memory scales linearly with context length — for a 70B model at 16-bit precision, storing 128K context requires roughly 80GB of GPU memory just for activations, before any computation happens. Second, attention distribution in most transformer variants is heavily weighted toward the beginning and end of sequences — a well-documented "lost in the middle" problem that means the middle of your context contributes less signal per token. Third, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines typically select only what fits, which means the quality of your context is bounded by a selection step, not by the full window size.

The result is tiered context quality. You have high-quality context (system prompt, recent turns, retrieved chunks), medium-quality context (summaries of older interactions), and effectively zero context (everything you had to drop because it did not fit). This looks a lot like a memory hierarchy.

### What memory locality means in AI terms

In classical systems, locality means organizing data access so the most frequently used data lives closest to the processor. In AI systems, locality means organizing context so the most relevant tokens are within the model's effective window — not its nominal one. RAG chunking strategies, conversation truncation policies, and system prompt compression are all attempts to engineer context locality under budget constraints.

Agents make this worse by producing context faster than they can consume it meaningfully. After 20 turns, the context history is mostly summary tokens — the original signals degraded.

### The compression step nobody talks about

Every production agent system I have examined has an informal compression or summarization step somewhere in the pipeline. Sometimes it is explicit: summarize the last 10 turns before passing them forward. Sometimes it is implicit: truncation at a fixed token budget. Either way, the context being processed at step N is a lossy reconstruction of steps 1 through N-1.

This is where the memory wall analogy sharpens. Virtual memory did not eliminate the need to manage memory — it made memory management a first-class engineering concern. Context windows will not eliminate the need to manage context — they will make context management a first-class concern, and most current tooling has not caught up.

### What changes if you accept the analogy

If context is like memory, the relevant skills are caching discipline, locality optimization, and graceful degradation under pressure. Context selection — deciding what enters the window and in what form — becomes the equivalent of a cache eviction policy. The "what changed my mind" signal in a long conversation is essentially a miss rate metric.

I do not have clean numbers on how often production contexts exceed their usable window size. But the tooling most teams reach for when an agent starts degrading over long sessions — context summarization, sliding window prompts, retrieval reranking — are all memory management techniques, not model improvements.

The memory wall did not stop compute from advancing. It just made certain uses of compute expensive relative to others. Context windows will not stop AI capability from advancing. They will make certain patterns of context use expensive relative to others — and the architectures and tools that win in the next few years will be the ones that treat context as a resource to be managed, not an input to be maximized.
